purpose: How much does a full spherical tank hold as its radius grows?
meaning: A sphere consists of points a fixed radius r from its center, and its enclosed ball has volume V=4πr³/3. The complete spherical surface has area A=4πr² and the diameter is d=2r. Radius changes length, surface and capacity at different rates: by the first, second and third powers of the scale factor.

definition.setting: An ideal full spherical tank has inner radius r metres. A cutaway view shows the center-to-wall radius, the diameter and the equatorial disk. Follow a radius change into the complete curved surface area and the full enclosed volume, with each quantity labeled in its own physical unit.

signature.r: Inner radius from tank center to the spherical wall, in metres
signature.d: Diameter through the tank center, in metres
signature.A: Complete spherical surface area, in square metres
signature.V: Enclosed volume of the full spherical tank, in cubic metres

conditions: The radius is positive, from 0.25 to 5 metres. The tank is exactly spherical and full. Surface area measures the complete ideal inner surface; volume measures its enclosed ball.
definition.domain_notes: The equatorial disk is a cross-section with area πr²; it is neither the sphere surface area nor its volume. Perspective and projection are illustrations, while all values come from the analytic Euclidean formulas. Wall thickness, supports, filling depth and practical construction are outside this full-tank model.

properties.derivation: The sphere surface area is four times its equatorial disk area πr². Integrating circular cross-sections from one pole to the other gives the enclosed volume 4πr³/3. As an independent numerical check, integrate the disk areas π(r²−x²) with Simpson quadrature, which is exact for this quadratic cross-section profile apart from floating-point rounding. Doubling r multiplies surface area by four and volume by eight.
